Context: StarRocks-on-Sirius (GPU SQL engine embedded in a StarRocks compute node, "CN"). An SF1000 profiling campaign found four blockers; you are helping choose the best fix for one of them.
Read first: /home/prestouser/.claude/plans/sf1000-top4-fixes-plan.md (the plan: issues, candidate solutions, criteria, acceptance tests) and the relevant findings in /home/prestouser/.claude/plans/starrocks-sirius-perf/sf1000-planning-cardinality-backpressure.md (sections 3B, 3C, 4). Evidence bundle: /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000 (WORKFLOW-PLAN.md indexes it; cn1-cnlog.txt, cn1-quent.txt, card-compare-*.txt, cn1/engine-cn0.log, cn1/dump/ are the raw material).
Source tree (read-only for you): /home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/perf (engine C++ under src/, CN Rust under experimental/starrocks/src, translator under experimental/starrocks/crates/starrocks-plan-translator, StarRocks FE Java under experimental/starrocks/starrocks/fe, engine docs under docs/super-sirius/).
Rules: do not modify the source tree, do not start clusters or GPU jobs, write only under /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/fix/designs/. Distinguish measured facts from inference. Cite file:line for every mechanism you rely on.

Issue: Make the six failing queries run on 1 CN (fusion, spill, or both). Findings to read: P1, B1, B2, P5 (RIGHT_SEMI gap). Code to read: compute_node_service.rs process_fragment/translate path and local_exchange register_receiver at the TPlan level; ExchangeNode row layout guarantees; translator join lowering; streaming_fragment.cpp output repositories; downgrade_executor tiers; sirius_ffi.cpp output_row_count/export_packed HOST-tier; which of the six each option rescues and at what cost.
Angle: what the maintainers of this repository (see CONTRIBUTING.md, docs/super-sirius/*.md, the carve plan conventions in the plan) would accept as a reviewable PR: fits existing abstractions, tests in the existing suites, no new knobs without a doc row, and clear layering (engine vs CN vs FE patch).
Produce ONE complete design: mechanism (what changes, in which functions, how it behaves under the measured SF1000 case and under the 15 passing queries), files to touch, tests (unit/component and the SF1000 acceptance), predicted effect with numbers derived from the evidence, risks, effort, dependencies on the other three fixes. Write your full design as markdown to /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/fix/designs/fragment-fusion-upstream.md (include the code excerpts you relied on with file:line) and return the structured summary.

- ooc-sort-dev: Use when developing, building, testing, or iterating on the disk-backed (out-of-core) sort implementation for cudf-polars in ~/bzaitlen/test-data/ooc-sort/. Covers installing into the rapidsmpf container env, running streaming sort tests, and the phase-by-phase implementation workflow.
- build-errors: Use this skill when the build fails, compilation errors occur, or you see undefined references, linker errors, CUDA compilation issues, missing headers, or template instantiation failures. Analyzes errors, suggests fixes, and iteratively rebuilds until success.
- build-sirius-starrocks: Build the Sirius-as-StarRocks-CN stack on a fresh GPU box — UCX, nixl, libsirius, StarRocks FE, and the Rust CN. Use when standing the stack up from scratch, recovering a broken toolchain (g++/ld/nvml shims, CUDA 13, no-root conda deps), applying the StarRocks proto patch, or relocating pixi/cargo/Maven onto local NVMe.
- cn-tuning: Size Sirius StarRocks CN memory and operator budgets for a given GPU box and TPC-H scale factor. Use when choosing GPU_MEM, STAGING, HOST_MEM, hash_partition_bytes, scan_task_batch_size, or when a query OOMs / exhausts the exchange arena / looks like an engine bug that is actually mis-sizing. Covers the derived-flag path vs a full sirius.yaml.
- dataset-manager: Use this skill to generate benchmark datasets (TPC-H, TPC-DS, etc.). Trigger when the user needs test data at a specific scale factor for benchmarking or testing. Supports parquet and duckdb output formats.
- log-analyzer: Use this skill to analyze Sirius query execution logs — to find why a query is slow, diagnose validation errors (wrong results), spot excessive downgrading, identify pipeline gaps, or compare two runs of the same query. Trigger whenever the user mentions a Sirius log file, says "look at this log", asks about per-operator time, pipeline gaps, memory pressure, downgrade behavior, validation/correctness mismatches, or wants to compare two query runs. Also use as a hand-off target from race-check (for two-run comparisons), runtime-errors (for "where did the query stall before hang"), and validate (for diffing the bad run against a good run). This is the log-only counterpart to profile-analyzer (nsys) and optimization-advisor (source-level guidance).
- module-context: Automatically identify which dependency library modules are relevant to a task and load their API documentation into context. Use PROACTIVELY before implementing features, fixing bugs, or writing new operators — analyzes the task description and loads cudf, rmm, duckdb, cucascade module docs to improve code quality. Trigger when the user asks to implement, add, fix, or modify GPU operators, pipeline components, memory management, joins, aggregations, sorting, expressions, or data I/O.
- module-discover: Discover and document a dependency library or submodule — analyzes all uses within the codebase, divides the library into logical modules, identifies which modules are used, and generates LLM-consumable API documentation for each module. Use when the user wants to understand a library dependency, map its modules, or generate API reference docs for a submodule.
- optimization-advisor: Use this skill to find exactly which source code to optimize for better GPU performance. Maps nsys profile hotspots to specific Sirius source files and functions, classifies bottlenecks as GPU-bound, CPU-bound, or sync-bound, and recommends actionable code changes. Trigger when the user wants to know what to optimize, where to focus coding effort, or wants source-level optimization guidance. This skill focuses on actionable source code targets — for generating performance reports and measurements, use profile-analyzer instead.
- pr-digest: Generates a "learning" PR-review digest — a markdown file at PR_digests/PR_digest_<N>.md that explains what a GitHub PR does, why, and exactly where in the code, with clickable file/line links and trimmed diffs. Use this whenever the user shares a GitHub PR URL (e.g. github.com/owner/repo/pull/1234) and wants to understand, summarize, review, walk through, or get up to speed on what changed — phrases like "can you review this PR", "what does this PR do", "help me understand this pull request", "summarize the changes in PR
- pre-commit-cleanup: Clean the current Git changes before committing. Use when preparing to commit or when the pre-commit cleanliness hook blocks a commit.
- profile-analyzer: Use this skill to understand why a Sirius query is slow, identify GPU bottlenecks, or detect performance regressions. Generates reports with kernel occupancy, memory bandwidth, operator attribution, and cross-run comparisons. Trigger when the user mentions profiling, nsys, GPU utilization, kernel analysis, performance reports, or wants to compare query timings across runs. This skill focuses on measurement and reporting — for mapping hotspots to source code fixes, use optimization-advisor instead.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.

1	# Plan: best solutions for the four SF1000 blockers, and the workflows that deliver them
2	
3	Written 2026-09-03 15:20 UTC from the report `starrocks-sirius-perf/sf1000-planning-cardinality-backpressure.md`
4	(sections 3B, 3C, 4). Evidence bundle: session scratchpad `perf/sf1000/` (indexed by `WORKFLOW-PLAN.md` there).
5	Working tree for all code: `/home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/fix-*` worktrees of the sirius-stacks clone,
6	one branch per fix off `perf/profile-sf1000` (45dab3be = d24f02c4 + aggregate gate + async dispatch + Quent probes).
7	Never the shared clone `/home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius`. No pushes, no PRs until asked.
8	
9	## The four issues
10	
11	| # | issue | where it lives | measured cost today (SF1000, 1 CN, 100 GiB pool) |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| 1 | The OOM reschedule loop has no feasibility check | `src/pipeline/gpu_pipeline_executor.cpp` (:263 reservation gate, :330-420 reschedule, MAX_RETRIES=100, 50 ms sleep) | q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21 take 54-232 s to die (775 s of a 910 s sweep); 17,917 "0 bytes freed, proceeding with partial reservation" lines |
14	| 2 | No per-query parked-output bookkeeping | `experimental/starrocks/src/engine.rs` (:291-316 process-wide wipe on Err), `compute_node_service.rs` (:449-476 cancel is result-store only), `local_exchange.rs` (removals only in take_ready) | 0-38 GB of a dead query's parked output survives into later queries; dead query's queued senders still run (q22 cold 4110 vs 943 ms) |
15	| 3 | The FE plans every FILES() scan at 1 row | StarRocks FE `StatisticsCalculator.computeFileScanNode` (:664-676), `TableFunctionTable.java` (file sizes at :611, schema RPC), `PGetFileSchemaResult` (proto :647-650), CN `file_schema.rs` | every distribution decision is data-blind: 1 CN broadcasts 3.79B lineitem rows into q04's semi join, 4 CNs shuffle 3.23B rows for q03; all six failures are one plan shape |
16	| 4 | Six queries cannot run on 1 CN | fragment cut (FE) + receiver-first full materialisation (`engine.rs` run_fragment_inner, `local_exchange.rs`) + parked repositories outside the downgrade sweep (`src/exec/streaming_fragment.cpp:103-112`, `src/downgrade/downgrade_executor.cpp:223-300`) | q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21 OOM; standalone Sirius runs them in 2.7-6.5 s |
17	
18	## Candidate solutions to weigh (input to the design workflow, not the decision)
19	
20	1. **Fail fast.** (a) Abort at the reservation gate when `retry_count > 0 && freed == 0 && retry floor > grant`; (b) abort in the reschedule path when downgrade freed 0 and pool usage == limit and nothing completed since the previous attempt; (c) a bounded wall-clock/attempt budget per original task that scales with observed progress; (d) keep 100 retries for the batch-lock contention case (arrives via `rmm::out_of_memory` from `lock_or_prepare_batch`, not via the gate). Must produce an error that names parked bytes vs pool.
21	2. **Bookkeeping.** (a) `query_id` on every `ParkedOutput`, drop only the failing query's slots; (b) failed-query set on the engine thread that skips pending `Run`s; (c) `cancel_plan_fragment` drops the cancelled query's parked outputs and dequeues its fragments (needs a by-query removal in `LocalExchange`); (d) `drop_parked` in `run_ready_fragment`'s Err arm for pre-run translation failures; (e) a periodic sweep as a safety net. Order of landing matters: (a)+(d) are pure hygiene, (b)/(c) touch the dispatch contract.
22	3. **Cardinalities.** (a) FE-only: rows = total bytes / row width from the inferred schema in `computeFileScanNode`, using `TableFunctionTable` file sizes (no wire change; column stats stay UNKNOWN); (b) exact `num_rows` from parquet footers: new field in `PGetFileSchemaResult`, filled by the CN's `file_schema.rs` (proto + FE + CN); (c) later, per-column min/max from row-group stats; (d) no-FE alternative: CN-side translator refusal/hints, SQL join hints. Delivered as a patch in `experimental/starrocks/patches/` applied by `apply-starrocks-patches.sh`, so the FE must be rebuilt (`pixi run fe-build`). Predicted effect must be checked with `EXPLAIN COSTS` at 1 and 4 CNs: the source skeptic warns that `BROADCAST_JOIN_MEM_EXCEED_PENALTY` and zero single-node shuffle cost may still put lineitem across an exchange on 1 CN.
23	4. **Run the six on 1 CN.** (a) Same-node fragment fusion before translation: replace a receiver's `EXCHANGE_NODE` with its single local sender's node list at the `TPlan` level when every destination is this CN, so the fused plan is the standalone plan (needs `RIGHT_SEMI` in the translator for q21, finding P5); (b) spillable parked repositories: register streaming-sink outputs and receiver inputs with a registry the downgrade executor sweeps as a third tier, HOST-tier `output_row_count` and `export_packed` (five of six then fit in GPU+HOST = 279 GB; q09 marginal); (c) streaming receivers (build side first, probe streamed) is the long-term fix but touches the engine's single-flight lifecycle; (d) FE-side: real cardinalities (issue 3) may already move lineitem to the probe side of a broadcast join, which the engine can stream. The design must say which combination actually makes each of the six pass and what each costs.
24	
25	## Evaluation criteria (judges score 1-5 each)
26	
27	1. Does it fix the measured failure at SF1000 on this box (which queries, predicted numbers, how verified)?
28	2. Correctness risk and blast radius (which paths change for the 15 passing queries; determinism; cancellation).
29	3. Size and reviewability as an upstream PR (target layer in the carve plan: engine `src/` -> dev PR; CN `experimental/starrocks` -> fork PR; FE -> checked-in patch), tests it needs.
30	4. Effort and dependencies (what must land first; FE rebuild; proto change).
31	5. Measurability: an acceptance test that a reviewer can rerun in minutes plus the SF1000 arm.
32	
33	## Acceptance tests (must exist before implementation is "done")
34	
35	| fix | unit / component test | SF1000 verification (orchestrator-run, one arm at a time) |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| 1 | Catch2 test in `test/cpp/pipeline/` driving a task through the reschedule path with a memory space that never frees: query fails within a bounded number of attempts with the new error text; contention case still retries | 1 CN, q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21: time-to-fail <= 5 s each (was 54-232 s), error names parked bytes; the 15 passing queries unchanged (warm medians within noise, `compare.py` set unchanged) |
38	| 2 | Rust tests in `engine.rs`/`local_exchange.rs`/`compute_node_service.rs`: failure drops only that query's slots; queued senders of a failed query are skipped; cancel drops parked outputs; translation failure drops slots in hand | 1 CN sweep in the same order as before: `[gpu_pool] allocated` returns to baseline after each failure (was +4.7..+38 GB), q22 cold no longer inflated, no `fragment run started` for a dead query after its failure |
39	| 3 | FE unit test (Java) for the new statistics path; CN test if the proto changes; `EXPLAIN COSTS` golden outputs for q03 q04 q05 q22 at 1 and 4 CNs showing real cardinalities and the new join sides | 1 CN and 4 CN sweeps of the 15 passing queries plus the six: plan shapes recorded, timings vs the campaign table, oracle compares |
40	| 4 | Fusion: translator/CN tests that a single-destination local exchange fuses and the fused plan matches the sender+receiver plan; spill: Catch2 test that a parked repository is swept to HOST and relayed back | 1 CN: q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21 pass with oracle MATCH; report their times against standalone (2.7-6.5 s) |
41	
42	## Workflows
43	
44	**A. Design exploration (`fix/design-workflow.js`).** Per issue, three independent designers with different angles (surgical minimum, robust design, what upstream would accept), each reads the report finding, the evidence and the code and returns a design (mechanism, files, tests, risks, predicted effect). Two judges per issue score the three against the criteria and pick or merge. One synthesizer per issue writes the spec `scratchpad/fix/designs/<issue>-SPEC.md`. A final integrator checks the four specs for interactions (fail-fast vs bookkeeping ordering; fusion vs spill vs cardinalities) and writes the build order.
45	
46	**B. Implementation (`fix/implement-workflow.js`).** Per issue in its own worktree: implementer (tests first, then code, build, run the unit tests; commits with Conventional Commits and the Claude trailer), adversarial reviewer, fixer, verifier (fresh build + tests + clippy/fmt/pre-commit). Agents never start clusters or use GPUs other than the one assigned to their worktree (fix 1: GPU 0, fix 2: GPU 1, fix 3: none, fix 4: GPU 2). The orchestrator then runs the SF1000 arms from the table above, one at a time, and an integration branch with all four for the final sweep.
47	
48	**C. Report.** `starrocks-sirius-perf/sf1000-top4-fixes-report.md`: per fix, what changed, tests, SF1000 before/after, what is left; plus the PR plan (branch, base, size) for when pushing is asked for.

# SF1000 profiling: planning / cardinality / backpressure — evidence bundle and analysis plan

Build: worktree /home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/perf, branch perf/profile-sf1000 = d24f02c4 + 85658f09 (aggregate gate) +
9a5a4da6 (async sender dispatch) + 45dab3be (Quent probes: scan_split_read, stream hops, staging leases, CN fragment labels).
Data: /scratch/sirius/datasets/tpch_sf1000 (decimal TPC-H, one parquet dir per table). Queries: experimental/starrocks/benchmarks/tpch/queries/qNN.sql.

## Evidence (scratchpad = /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000)
- survey/explain/qNN.costs.txt, qNN.verbose.txt   FE EXPLAIN COSTS / VERBOSE for all 22 queries (fragments, join distribution, cardinality: 1 everywhere)
- survey/plan-summary.txt                          explain_summary.py over all 22 (joins with build/probe children and broadcast tables)
- cn1/  cn4/  standalone/                           the three arms; each has runs/runs.csv (query,run,phase,status,ms,rows,start_utc), runs/qNN.rK.out(.err)
- cn1/cluster.log, cn4/cluster.log                  FE + CN logs (fragment run started/finished, declared input stream cardinality, relayed batches, transmitted batches via nixl, OOM reschedule warnings)
- cn1/dump/fragment-*.txt, plan-*.substrait         every fragment the FE sent to the 1-CN and the translator's Substrait plan
- cn1/quent/.cnN/<session>/, cn4/quent/.cnN/<session>/, standalone/quent/<session>/   Quent ndjson (task FSM, data_batch, batch_placement, memory, scan_split_read)
- standalone/runs/qNN.explain.txt                   DuckDB/Sirius EXPLAIN of the same SQL (the stats-aware planner's choice)
- <arm>-cnlog.json (cnlog_extract.py), <arm>-quent.txt / .json (quent_bp.py), card-compare-<arm>.txt (card_compare.py), results.md (results_table.py)
- ../../oracle/tpch_sf1000/qNN.tsv                  DuckDB CPU oracle answers; compare-*.txt

## Tools (same dir)
explain_summary.py, cnlog_extract.py, card_compare.py, quent_bp.py, results_table.py, ../quent_summary.py (per-operator Computing sums)

## Facts established before the analysis
1. FE StatisticsCalculator.computeFileScanNode sets outputRowCount = 1 for FILES() scans ("we don't know the real schema in file, just use the default Row Count now"); every column statistic UNKNOWN. Hence every plan node has cardinality 1 and the CBO picks BROADCAST for most joins (orders 1.5B rows broadcast in q07/q09/q10..., lineitem 3.79B rows as the build side of q04's LEFT SEMI JOIN, partsupp 800M in q02).
2. Engine stream ids == FE exchange node ids; the receiver declares the exact parked row count per stream before build() ("declared input stream cardinality"), so DuckDB plans the receiver fragment with exact input cardinalities, but only after every sender finished (receiver-first rendezvous, local_exchange.rs). Nothing streams across a fragment boundary: the whole intermediate is parked on the GPU.
3. Engine OOM handling: gpu_pipeline_executor.cpp reschedules a task on OOM up to MAX_RETRIES=100 with a 50 ms sleep, then fails the query ("exceeded maximum retry limit"). It does not wait for memory to be released and cannot spill parked batches. q05 and q08 died this way on 1 CN at SF1000 (GPU_SCAN OOM, 101 s and 168 s).
4. Reserving.requested_bytes / peak_estimate vs Computing.peak_allocated_bytes (Quent task FSM) measure the engine's own memory estimation; standalone SF10 q01 requested 20.8 GB for a 5.6 GB peak.

## Analysis dimensions (workflow)
A. Planning: per query, FE fragment tree and join distribution vs the DuckDB/Sirius standalone plan; what a stats-aware FE would choose; where the translator/CN could override (e.g. swap build/probe, refuse broadcast above a row threshold, local re-planning of a broadcast join once the actual parked cardinality is known).
B. Cardinality: FE estimate vs actual rows per exchange (card_compare), engine reservation estimate vs peak (quent_bp), the receiver-first exact-cardinality mechanism and its cost.
C. Backpressure: parked bytes and dwell per fragment, staging lease held/in-transit time and max concurrency vs SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_BYTES, Reserving/Queued waits, OOM reschedule storms, nixl transmit lease_ms/write_ms, 1-CN vs 4-CN scaling per query, standalone vs CN.
Each per-query analysis is verified adversarially (two skeptics with different lenses); the synthesis ranks findings with the evidence lines and proposes changes with file paths and confidence.

## Facts added after the 1-CN sweep (13:19 UTC)
5. Supported on the CN path at SF1000 (1 CN, 100 GiB pool): q01 q02 q03 q04 q06 q07 q10 q11 q12 q13 q14 q15 q19 q20 q22 pass (15). Fail: q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21 = OOM at GPU_SCAN after 100 reschedules
   (101 s, 168 s, 232 s, 104 s, 54 s, 114 s to die; 2500-5600 reschedule warnings each, see cn1-cnlog.txt); q16 = translator gap ("multi_distinct_count has a partial state this translator does not model").
6. q15 returned 0 rows in run 1 and 1 row in runs 0 and 2 on 1 CN: streams 18 and 22 (the revenue = max(revenue) join output) carried 0 rows in run 1 while every other stream was identical.
   The build has the canonical float-sum sort gated OFF (SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS unset), so the two independently computed FP64 sums can differ in the last bits. Follow-up arms cn1-canon-q15 / cn1-nocanon-q15 test this.
7. Engine executor pools default to pipeline num_threads: 4 (docs/super-sirius/configuration.md:91-94); Quent "Queued" time per fragment is the wait for one of those slots plus the memory reservation gate.
   1-CN q04: scan fragment 37 tasks, Queued sum 19.9 s vs Computing 4.7 s inside a 1.2 s wall; join fragment requested 253 GB of reservations for a 61 GB summed peak (4x over-estimate).
8. Translator comment (node_translator.rs ~1924-1931) already records that the FE reports cardinality 1 for every FILES() scan and that nothing bounds a join build side; "bounding it belongs to the executor".
9. FE plans with 4 CNs alive are in survey/explain4/ (plan-summary-4cn.txt); diff against plan-summary.txt shows whether node count changes any distribution decision.
10. Plan-node enum decode for the dumps (TPlanNodeType(N)): survey/TPlanNodeType.map.txt (4 HASH_JOIN, 6 AGGREGATION, 8 SORT, 9 EXCHANGE, 17 FILE_SCAN, 28 PROJECT, ...).
11. The engine's DuckDB optimizer runs on every fragment (sirius_ffi.cpp:135, with STATISTICS_PROPAGATION and a few rewrites disabled, :233-240); the declared stream cardinality feeds the TableFunction cardinality callback (stream_bind_catalog.hpp:44-46), so build/probe choice inside a fragment sees exact stream sizes, but FILES() scans inside the same fragment carry DuckDB's parquet estimate. The FE's fragment cut (what is broadcast/shuffled) is fixed before any of this.
12. The FE's plan DEPENDS on the number of alive CNs even with cardinality 1 everywhere: with 4 CNs most joins flip from BROADCAST to PARTITIONED (shuffle) and fragment counts rise (q02 13->16, q08 11->16, q09 9->12; q03 orders join BROADCAST->PARTITIONED; q04/q12/q14/q19 BROADCAST->PARTITIONED; q15 -> BUCKET_SHUFFLE). survey/plan-summary.txt (1 CN) vs survey/plan-summary-4cn.txt (4 CNs); card-compare-cn4.txt uses the 4-CN plans (q03 exch2 = 3.23B lineitem rows shuffled, q12 exch1 = 1.5B orders rows shuffled).
13. 4-CN staging leases per query (cn4-quent.txt, attributed by time): q07.r1 747 leases / 141.5 GB moved / 92.9 s summed lease-held time inside a 1.79 s query, max 64 concurrent leases per CN; q04.r1 360 leases / 48.8 GB; q01.r1 14 leases / 0.06 GB. Session-wide per CN ~3700 leases, max 94 concurrent (arena = 16 GiB).
14. Standalone (one GPU, 100 GiB pool, DuckDB planner with parquet statistics) runs the same 15 queries; standalone/runs/qNN.explain.txt holds its plans. 1-CN vs standalone warm medians (ms): q01 5073/4882, q02 1246/571, q03 3106/3050, q07 3476/3266, q11 970/336, q15 4685/2627, q20 4171/3023, q22 943/496 (results.md).
15. Pre-digested tables added: reservation-ratio.txt (per run: tasks, summed reservation request vs summed measured peak, ratio, summed Queued and Computing seconds, wall; cn1 q11 54x, q14 15x, q03 14x, q10 6x over-reservation), cn4-transmits.txt (nixl transmits per run: count, GB, elapsed/lease/write ms, write GB/s).
16. Correctness vs the DuckDB oracle (compare-cn1.txt, compare-cn4.txt, compare-standalone.txt; rel tol 1e-6): standalone 15/15 MATCH. CN arms: q02 q04 q06 q12 q13 q14 q20 q22 MATCH; q01 q07 q19 differ by 9.6e-4 and q03 by 1.8e-3 in revenue sums (the known `1 - 0.07` FP64->DECIMAL(16,2) truncation from #1236's lowering, not a multi-CN defect); q10 differs with maxreldiff 12.3 over 48 cells of its 20 rows, most likely the same truncated revenue sums reordering the TOP-20 (verify by comparing the customer sets and the revenue column); q15 differs by 1.1e-3 on its single row and is also flaky in row count (see fact 6); q11 shows EMPTY because the query returns 0 rows at SF1000 on both engines (the bench kit does not scale q11's 0.0001 fraction by 1/SF), so it is not a defect but the compare cannot confirm it.
17. results-ratios.md: 1-CN parity T_sr1/T_standalone is 0.95-1.2 for the scan-heavy queries (q01 q03 q04 q06 q07 q12 q14 q19), 1.2-1.4 for q10 q13 q20, and 1.8-2.9 for the fragment-heavy small ones (q02 2.18, q11 2.88, q15 1.78, q22 1.90); 4-CN speed-up over 1 CN is 1.7-2.35x (efficiency 0.43-0.59) for the scan-heavy queries and 1.08-1.46x for q02 q11 q22.
18. Follow-up arms (may still be running while you work; use them only if their files exist): standalone-failed/runs/runs.csv (standalone Sirius on q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21), cn1-canon-q15/runs/runs.csv (1 CN, SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS=1, 6 runs of q15) vs cn1-nocanon-q15/runs/runs.csv (gate off).
19. DONE: standalone Sirius (same GPU, same 100 GiB pool, DuckDB planner with parquet statistics, pipelined execution) runs every query the CN path could not: q05 5191/2786 ms (pass, rows=5), q08 3835/3674 ms (pass, rows=2), q09 6818/5427 ms (pass, rows=175), q17 4386/3786 ms (pass, rows=1), q18 2764/2691 ms (pass, rows=100), q21 6534/6401 ms (pass, rows=100) (cold/warm; standalone-failed/runs/runs.csv, plans in standalone-failed/runs/qNN.explain.txt, Quent in standalone-failed/quent/). The CN path died on the same queries after 54-232 s of OOM reschedules. This is the central planning + backpressure contrast of the campaign.
20. DONE q15 determinism A/B on 1 CN (6 runs each): SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS=1 -> rows per run ['0', '1', '0', '0', '1', '0'] (ms ['10331', '5161', '5182', '5002', '4876', '4809']); gate off -> rows ['0', '0', '1', '0', '0', '0'] (ms ['10576', '4795', '4847', '4799', '4661', '4788']). Files: cn1-canon-q15/, cn1-nocanon-q15/ (runs, cluster.log, quent, engine-*.log).
21. CORRECTION to fact 6: the A/B in fact 20 REFUTES the simple hypothesis that the SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS gate alone explains q15's empty runs: with the canonical sort ON, 4 of 6 runs still return 0 rows (gate off: 5 of 6). The gate only canonicalizes row order inside the update-phase aggregate; the FE plan computes the revenue CTE twice (two independent two-phase aggregations over FP64-lowered decimals) and then joins on `total_revenue = max(total_revenue)`. Batch arrival order into the merge phase (and therefore FP64 summation order) still varies run to run, so the two sums can differ in the last bits and the equality join yields nothing. # Super Sirius Documentation

Super Sirius is the new task-based GPU execution engine in Sirius. It uses `namespace sirius` and replaces the legacy `gpu_processing` path with a pipelined, multi-threaded architecture that partitions work across GPU and CPU thread pools.

With a Sirius config file (`~/.sirius/sirius.yaml`), GPU execution is **transparent** — users write plain SQL and supported queries automatically execute on the GPU. Unsupported queries silently fall back to CPU. The explicit `CALL gpu_execution('...')` function is still available but no longer required. Legacy `sirius.cfg` is still recognized for compatibility.

```sql
-- Just load the extension. If ~/.sirius/sirius.yaml exists, GPU is automatic.
LOAD 'sirius.duckdb_extension';

-- Plain SQL — transparently executed on GPU:
SELECT l_returnflag, SUM(l_quantity) FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_returnflag;
```

## How It Differs from Legacy Sirius

| Aspect | Legacy (`gpu_processing`) | Super Sirius |
|--------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Namespace | `duckdb` | `sirius` |
| Entry point | `CALL gpu_processing(...)` | Plain SQL (transparent) or `CALL gpu_execution(...)` |
| Plan generator | `GPUPhysicalPlanGenerator` | `sirius_physical_plan_generator` |
| Operators | `GPUPhysicalOperator` in `src/operator/` | `sirius_physical_operator` in `src/op/` |
| Execution model | Single-threaded GPU executor | Multi-pipeline task-based execution |
| Memory management | `GPUBufferManager` | cuCascade tiered memory (GPU/Host/Disk) |

## Table of Contents

| Document | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| [Architecture Overview](architecture-overview.md) | Component diagram, thread model, ownership hierarchy, execution lifecycle |
| [Execution Flow](execution-flow.md) | End-to-end query trace with file:line references |
| [Physical Plan Generation](physical-plan-generation.md) | Logical-to-physical mapping, pipeline construction, splitting rules |
| [Operators](operators.md) | All physical operators: interface, GPU implementation, cuDF APIs |
| [Expression Evaluator](expression-executor.md) | `expression_evaluator`, Sirius AST hierarchy, GPU expression translator, cuDF AST |
| [Pipeline Execution](pipeline-execution.md) | GPU executor, task scheduling, completion, OOM handling, per-task-device contract under SCHED-RR |
| [Task Creator](task-creator.md) | Task creation: hint chain, per-operator scheduling behavior |
| [Scan](scan.md) | Scan subsystem: unified GPU scan operator, `gpu_ingestible` (parquet + DuckDB-native), scan manager, pinned tables, DuckDB-native decode, row-group pruning, Sirius IO layer (uring/REST/kvikio + prefetching cache) |
| [Memory Management](memory-management.md) | cuCascade tiers, reservations, downgrade executor |
| [Data Management](data-management.md) | Data batches, repositories, ports, barrier semantics |
| [Streaming Sessions](streaming-sessions.md) | Fragment boundaries for distributed queries: `exec::batch_stream`, streaming source/sink, partition fan-out (broadcast / hash-key), the id-addressed `stream_session` |
| [Streaming Fragments](streaming-fragments.md) | Building and running one fragment: `stream_bind_catalog`, `exec::streaming_fragment`, the cross-language `sirius::ffi::Fragment`/`Context` lifecycle |
| [Data Size Estimation](data-size-estimation.md) | Runtime projection of the total bytes that will reach an operator's input port |
| [Configuration](configuration.md) | sirius_config, operator_params, SET variables |
| [Optimizations](optimizations.md) | Performance optimizations with PRs, code paths, configs |
| [Compressed Pinning](compressed-pinning.md) | Simpatico-compressed pin_table on host/GPU tiers — which tier to compress on, plan selection vs the H2D link, GB300 SF1000 results |
| [Compressed Materialization](compressed-materialization.md) | Value-preserving narrow integer and DECIMAL carriers, restoration boundaries, and pin-cache invariants |
| [Multi-GPU Architecture](multi-gpu-architecture.md) | How Sirius executes SQL across every GPU on a node — tiers, pin tables, ready-device scheduling, cross-GPU transfers, downgrade, concurrency invariants |
| [Late Materialization](late-materialization.md) | Carrying a pin-order rowid instead of wide column values — the scan/port pair, group-by-rowid rides, riders, the pin-time uniqueness proof, and the `SIRIUS_EXP_LATE_MAT_*` gates |
| [Dynamic Filters](dynamic-filters.md) | Ordered hash-build publication, zone-map/IN-list/Bloom consumers, multi-GPU replicas, join-edge (SIP) endpoint placement, and the refinement design that remains future work |
| [Debugging](debugging.md) | Practical guide to debugging crashes and races — building/running with ASan & TSan, the `tsan.supp` file, and capturing/inspecting core dumps with gdb |

## Suggested Reading Order

1. **Architecture Overview** — understand the component layout and thread model
2. **Execution Flow** — trace a query end-to-end through the system
3. **Physical Plan Generation** — how DuckDB logical plans become Sirius pipelines
4. **Operators** — what each operator does on the GPU
5. **Expression Evaluator** — how expressions are evaluated on GPU
6. **Pipeline Execution** — how tasks are dispatched and executed
7. **Task Creator** — how the system decides when to create tasks
8. **Scan** — how data enters the system from storage
9. **Memory Management** — GPU memory tiers, reservations, spilling
10. **Data Management** — data batch lifecycle and port wiring
11. **Streaming Sessions** — how a fragment's data enters and leaves when the query spans nodes

109:### 3A. Planning
111:#### P1 (confirmed). The six 1-CN failures are one FE plan shape: an unfiltered lineitem leaf feeding a hash-partitioned exchange, whose whole output must be parked on the GPU
144:#### P2 (confirmed). q02: the FE decorrelates the min-subquery into a full 800M-row partsupp chain and shuffles a 1-row region; its runtime filters are dropped by the CN
158:#### P3 (confirmed with a corrected mechanism). The FE's BROADCAST vs SHUFFLE choice is data-blind; on 4 CNs it shuffles the large table and keeps only narrow-key broadcasts
184:#### P4 (confirmed, impact narrowed). Every CN statement pays a fixed ~120-270 ms before the first fragment runs
203:#### P5 (not adversarially verified). Semi/anti join sides, CTE inlining, lost operator fusion, dropped dynamic filters

220:### 3B. Cardinality
222:#### C1 (confirmed). Every FE estimate is 1 row; actuals reach 6.0e9
234:#### C2 (confirmed). The receiver-first exact cardinality mechanism is correct but arrives too late and is undermined by a flat 0.2 selectivity on the FE's `IS NOT NULL` conjunct
240:#### C3 (confirmed, one correction). The engine's own reservation estimate is exact once a pipeline has history, but the cold-start estimate is 8x, and four cold-start scan tasks reserve 58-80% of the pool
254:### 3C. Backpressure
256:#### B1 (confirmed). Receiver-first rendezvous plus one fragment at a time turn every exchange into a full GPU materialisation
268:#### B2 (confirmed, mechanism sharpened). Parked batches are invisible to the downgrade sweep, so every OOM cycle frees 0 bytes although a 160 GiB HOST tier is configured
280:#### B3 (confirmed). The reschedule loop has no feasibility check: 179 stuck scan tasks x 100 retries x 50 ms, re-reading the split each time, while nothing can free memory
299:#### B4 (disputed: mechanism confirmed, causal claim refuted). Fragments of a failed query keep running and park output nobody consumes; the leak is 0-38 GB per failure but decided no pass/fail here

content.content:
# Fragments

A **fragment** is one runnable piece of a (possibly multi-node) query: a bound plan, its declared
input/output streams, and the machinery to build, run, and drain it. [Streaming
Sessions](streaming-sessions.md) covers the low-level primitives a fragment is built on
(`exec::batch_stream`, `STREAMING_SOURCE`/`STREAMING_SINK`, the id-addressed `exec::stream_session`
router). This document covers the layer above: how a Substrait or DuckDB plan becomes a fragment,
how its declared streams get a schema before the plan is even bound, and how multiple fragments —
possibly owned by different processes — chain together via `relay_from()`.

Two classes do this, at two different layers:

| | `exec::streaming_fragment` | `sirius::ffi::Fragment` |
|---|---|---|
| **Files** | `src/include/exec/streaming_fragment.hpp`, `src/exec/streaming_fragment.cpp` | `src/include/sirius_ffi.hpp`, `src/sirius_ffi.cpp` |
| **Caller** | C++ code already inside a live `duckdb::ClientContext` and transaction (e.g. the transparent path, `Context::execute_substrait`) | Any caller that must not include DuckDB/cuDF headers — the Rust bindings, or a standalone C++ embedder |
| **Owns the connection?** | No — borrows the caller's `ClientContext` | Yes — brings up its own embedded `duckdb::DuckDB` + `Connection` (`Context`) |
| **Transaction / query window** | Caller's responsibility to bracket | Manages its own, internally, across two phases (see below) |
| **Shape** | One output-only or gather sink; `spec.plan_source` is a `LogicalOperator` factory | Declare → build → relay → run, addressable by stream id from outside the process |

`sirius::ffi::Fragment` is a PIMPL wrapper around exactly one `exec::streaming_fragment` (or, for a
result fragment, around the single-shot `sirius_interface` path) — it exists to give a
cross-language caller everything `streaming_fragment` needs (a connection, a transaction, a query
window, a bind catalog) without exposing any of it.

## Quick path

```cpp
// exec::streaming_fragment — caller already owns the transaction/window.
fragment_spec spec;
spec.plan_source = my_plan_source;     // ClientContext& -> LogicalOperator
spec.outputs     = {0};                // one output stream
streaming_fragment frag(client, std::move(spec));
frag.build(query_id);
frag.run();                            // blocks
drain(frag.session(), 0);              // pull() until drained
```

```cpp
// sirius::ffi::Fragment — cross-language, owns everything.
auto ctx = make_context();
auto sender = make_fragment(*ctx);
sender->declare_output(0);
sender->build(substrait_plan_bytes);   // opens + closes its own setup transaction
sender->run();                         // blocks; closes the query lifecycle

auto receiver = make_fragment(*ctx);
receiver->declare_input_column(0, "a", "BIGINT");
receiver->build(other_plan_bytes);     // this plan reads sirius_stream_source(0) / view sirius_stream_0
receiver->relay_from(*sender, /*source_stream_id=*/0, /*input_stream_id=*/0, /*sender_id=*/0);
receiver->run();
```

## `stream_bind_catalog` + `sirius_stream_source` — bridging bind time and plan time

**Files:** `src/include/exec/stream_bind_catalog.hpp`, `src/exec/stream_bind_catalog.cpp`,
`src/include/exec/stream_plan_bindings.hpp`, `src/exec/stream_plan_bindings.cpp`

A fragment's input streams do not exist as DuckDB tables — there is nothing in the catalog for the
binder to look up. `sirius_stream_source(id)`, a table function, stands in for one: its **bind**
resolves a declared stream's schema (names + types) so the binder is satisfied; its **body never
runs** — the physical plan generator replaces every `sirius_stream_source` scan with a
`STREAMING_SOURCE` operator before execution. A plan does not call the function directly; it reads
`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW main.sirius_stream_<id> AS SELECT * FROM sirius_stream_source(<id>)`, so a
Substrait or SQL plan sees an ordinary-looking view name (`stream_view_name(id)` gives callers that
exact string).

Bind time and plan time are far apart — DuckDB binds a table function long before physical planning
runs — so both sides need a shared place to look up a declared stream's schema. That place is
`stream_bind_catalog`, a `duckdb::ClientContextState` registered per-connection:

```cpp
class stream_bind_catalog : public duckdb::ClientContextState {
 public:
  static constexpr const char* kStateKey = "sirius_stream_catalog";

  void declare(stream_id_t id, stream_input_binding binding);  // overwrites same-id entry
  void clear();                                                 // drop every declaration
  void erase(stream_id_t id);                                   // drop one; no-op if absent

  const stream_input_binding& get(stream_id_t id) const;        // @throws if undeclared
  void set_built(stream_id_t id, op::sirius_physical_streaming_source* built);
};

// Shared by every call site that needs "the catalog on this connection, or a clear error why not".
duckdb::shared_ptr<stream_bind_catalog> catalog_for(duckdb::ClientContext& context);
```

The round trip:

```
declare_input_column(id, name, type) × N   ── caller-side, before build() ──►  stream_bind_catalog::declare(id, ...)
                                                                                          │
stream_source_bind()  (DuckDB bind, resolves the CREATE VIEW's schema)  ◄── catalog_for(context)->get(id)
                                                                                          │
create_streaming_source_plan()  (physical planning, builds STREAMING_SOURCE)  ◄── catalog_for(context)->get(id)
                                                                                          │
                                                                                catalog->set_built(id, source.get())
                                                                                          │
streaming_fragment::build() / Fragment::build()  ── reads catalog->get(id).built ──►  session().add_source(id, *built)
```

`set_built()` is how the physical operator (created deep inside `create_plan()`, which does not
otherwise return anything the fragment layer can see) gets back to the session that wires it up.

### Contracts

- **Multiple fragments may share one connection at once.** A `Context` in the FFI layer can host
  several live `Fragment` objects — that is the whole point of `relay_from()` chaining several
  fragments together. `clear()` drops *every* declaration on the connection and is only safe for a
  caller that owns the whole catalog outright; a fragment that shares a connection with a peer must
  use `erase()`, which touches only the ids it declared itself. Both `streaming_fragment` (its
  destructor and the start of `build()`, for idempotent rebuilds) and `sirius::ffi::Fragment::Impl`
  follow this discipline — neither ever calls `clear()`.
- **A declared stream may be read by at most one plan leaf.** `set_built()` rejects a second bind
  for an id that already has one, instead of silently overwriting the pointer. Without this guard,
  a plan that reads the same declared stream twice (a self-join, or two independent scans of one
  shared subexpression) would silently orphan the first leaf: only the *last* bind's operator ends
  up registered with the session, so the earlier one never receives a push or a close and its
  pipeline waits forever with no error anywhere. Fan-out reads of one declared stream are not
  supported; if a plan genuinely needs that, feed each reader its own stream id instead.
- **The catalog must exist before any bind can succeed.** Both the transparent (normal SQL)
  connection path and the FFI's own embedded connection install a `stream_bind_catalog` when the
  connection opens — `SiriusContextExtensionCallback::OnConnectionOpened` for the former,
  `Context::Impl::bring_up()` for the latter — and remove it on close/teardown. Without this,
  `catalog_for()` throws immediately on the first `sirius_stream_source` bind or
  `streaming_fragment::build()` call.

## `exec::streaming_fragment` — plan builder + blocking runner

Owns one fragment's complete life cycle: declares inputs into the catalog, plans, constructs the
sink, runs, and keeps the output pullable after `run()` returns.

```cpp
struct fragment_spec {
  logical_plan_source plan_source;                    // ClientContext& -> LogicalOperator
  std::map<stream_id_t, stream_input_spec> inputs;     // schema + expected senders per input
  std::vector<stream_id_t> outputs;                    // positional: outputs[i] = partition i
  std::optional<op::partition_spec> partitioning;       // absent = single destination
  std::optional<std::string> query_label;              // Quent Query instance_name
  std::optional<std::string> session_label;            // Quent QueryGroup selector
};
```

`query_label` / `session_label` name the fragment's telemetry query (see
[Quent telemetry](quent-telemetry.md#query-labels)): absent, the engine reports
`sirius_streaming_fragment` in its default query group. The FFI's `Fragment::set_query_label`
fills them, and passes the same `query_label` as the execution-window label so the engine log's
window lines and the Quent Query agree.

**Construction validates the spec eagerly:** a plan source is required, at least one output stream
is required (a fragment with none is not this class's job — see the FFI's *result fragment* below),
and more than one output requires a `partitioning` mode (a bare `N`-output gather sink would leave
`N-1` streams permanently empty with no way to tell a caller why).

**`build(query_id)`** erases (not clears — see above) this fragment's own catalog ids, redeclares
them so a rebuild after a caught, corrected failure is idempotent, runs `plan_source` to get a
bound `LogicalOperator`, lowers it to a physical plan, and roots that plan in one
`sirius_physical_streaming_sink`:

- **Hash-key cast normalization.** When `partitioning`'s `key_cast_types` is left empty, `build()`
  derives one per key column so independently-planned senders always hash the same logical value
  identically — cuDF's `murmur3` hashes raw bytes, and an `INT32` sender vs. an `INT64` sender for
  the same column would otherwise split matching keys across different partitions. `TINYINT`/
  `SMALLINT`/`INTEGER` normalize to `INT64`; `BIGINT`/`BOOLEAN`/`VARCHAR` need no cast (`EMPTY`);
  `DECIMAL` normalizes to `FLOAT64`; anything else throws. A key column outside the sink's own
  column range throws before any cast is even attempted.
- Every declared input is checked against the catalog's `built` pointer after planning: a stream
  declared but never read by the plan throws immediately (a silent hang otherwise — nothing would
  ever close it).
- The engine owns the plan and the fragment owns the engine, so the sink (and its output
  repositories) stay pullable after `run()` returns — the query window's mandatory cleanup never
  touches them.

**Member declaration order is the lifetime contract.** C++ destroys members in reverse declaration
order, and `streaming_fragment` relies on it: repositories are declared first (so they outlive
everything that could still be writing to or reading from them), the engine next (it owns the
physical plan, which holds raw pointers into the operators the session also points at), and
`_session` last — so it is torn down *first*, before the engine it borrows operator pointers from
can go away. Reordering these members is a use-after-free waiting to happen, not a style choice.

**`run()`** reuses the caller's query window rather than opening a second one (a second
`StandaloneQueryScope` would reset the task creator and scan manager `build()` already populated,
and the fragment would run zero tasks). On any exception from the engine, it poisons every declared
output (`_session.fail_output(id, ...)`, swallowing secondary failures per id) **before**
rethrowing — otherwise a peer parked in `wait()` on that stream would block forever with no error
anywhere, the same S2/S3 hazard [Streaming Sessions](streaming-sessions.md#execbatch_stream)
documents for `batch_stream` itself. `fail_output()` is idempotent (first failure wins), so this is
safe to do at this layer even when a caller above it (`sirius::ffi::Fragment::run()`) also poisons
the same outputs — see [Other contracts](#other-contracts) below.

**`sink_types()`** exposes the plan root's output column types, set during `build()`. Relay steps
use it to validate schema agreement (column count and type ids) against a target fragment's
declared input types before any batch moves.

## `sirius::ffi::Fragment` — the cross-language lifecycle

**Files:** `src/include/sirius_ffi.hpp`, `src/sirius_ffi.cpp`

`Context` is an RAII handle to one embedded engine: its own `duckdb::SiriusContext`, its own
`duckdb::DuckDB` + `Connection`, and its own `stream_bind_catalog` — everything a fragment needs,
brought up once and shared by every `Fragment` created on it via `make_fragment(context)`.

`Fragment` is either an **intermediate** fragment (has declared output streams, rooted in a
`STREAMING_SINK`, wraps one `exec::streaming_fragment`) or a **result** fragment (no declared
outputs, executes once via `sirius_interface` and produces Arrow through `result_to_arrow()`).
Which one a `Fragment` becomes is decided implicitly, by whether `declare_output()` was ever
called (`is_result() == outputs.empty()`) — there is no separate constructor flag.

### `build()`: two phases, two different windows

```
declare_input_column / declare_input_sender / declare_output / declare_output_broadcast / declare_output_hash_key
                                          │
                                          ▼
                          ┌─── Phase 1: setup transaction ───┐
                          │  BeginTransaction()               │
                          │  resolve_inputs()   (type-name parsing — needs a catalog lookup)
                          │  declare_streams()  (populate stream_bind_catalog)
                          │  create_stream_views()  (CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW per input, real DDL)
                          │  Commit()                          │
                          └────────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
                                          ▼
                          ┌─── Phase 2: query window ─────────┐
                          │  StandaloneQueryScope acquired     │
                          │  partition-mode guard               │
                          │  is_result() ? single-shot execute-plan path
                          │              : construct + build() an exec::streaming_fragment
                          └────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Phase 1 exists because parsing a DuckDB type name and creating a view both need an active
transaction, and that transaction **must be committed before Phase 2 begins** — `StandaloneQueryScope`
acquires the engine's single-flight lifecycle slot, and the two are sequential, not nested. This is
also why a `Fragment::build()` failure can fall into two different states depending on *which*
phase it fails in:

- A failure during Phase 1 (a bad type name, a stream id that fails to bind at `CREATE VIEW` time)
  leaves the transaction open — `transaction_open` was set the instant `BeginTransaction()` returned
  and is only cleared once `Commit()` itself succeeds.
- A failure during Phase 2 happens with the transaction already closed; only the query-window slot
  needs releasing.

3:This document covers the memory tier hierarchy, reservation system, downgrade executor, and pinned host memory management.
7:Super Sirius uses cuCascade for tiered memory management across three tiers:
22:Each tier has configurable thresholds:
27:| `downgrade_trigger_fraction` | 0.8 | 0.9 | When to start downgrading |
28:| `downgrade_stop_fraction` | 0.6 | 0.8 | When to stop downgrading; configuration requires `0 < stop < trigger <= 1` |
38:- Bridges Sirius' task execution with cuCascade's tiered memory management
49:downgrade_trigger_fraction = 0.8;
50:downgrade_stop_fraction = 0.6;
57:downgrade_trigger_fraction = 0.9;
58:downgrade_stop_fraction = 0.8;
67:mount_paths;                    // directories for spill files
68:memory_capacity = 1TB;          // total spill capacity
89:Conversions that land data on the HOST tier draw down a caller-owned reservation instead of double-committing host capacity: the caller obtains a reservation with `make_reservation_or_null(size)` and passes it to the reservation-taking `convert_to`/`clone_to` overloads, so the converter's allocation is charged against capacity the caller already holds. If the reservation cannot be made, the call falls back — with a warning — to the `memory_space*` overload (no reservation; the converter may OOM). Call sites: `lock_or_prepare_batch` in `src/include/pipeline/batch_lock_utils.hpp` and the materialized result collector (`src/op/sirius_physical_result_collector.cpp`). The `memory_space*` overloads remain the path for GPU/DISK targets and viability probes.
91:## Downgrade Executor
93:**File:** `src/include/downgrade/downgrade_executor.hpp`, `src/downgrade/downgrade_executor.cpp`
95:One `downgrade_executor` per memory space monitors pressure and moves data to lower tiers.
99:- **Processing thread**: dequeues `downgrade_request` objects sequentially from an `interruptible_mpmc` queue
100:- **Monitor thread** (if `monitor_period > 0`): each cycle, if the memory space reports `should_downgrade_memory()`, it applies a **stateless viability gate** (`has_viable_downgrade_target()`) before enqueuing. A request is only fired when a lower tier could plausibly accept the data:
101:  - A configured DISK tier is always a viable target.
102:  - Without DISK, only a GPU source has a lower tier (HOST). Viability is confirmed by probing each HOST space with a chunk-sized `make_reservation_or_null` (released immediately) — the ground truth for whether downgraded data can actually land, since HOST capacity reflects both live reservations and already-stored downgraded data.
103:  - If no target is viable (e.g. idle GPU batches whose only lower tier is a full HOST with no DISK configured), the monitor **backs off** for that cycle without enqueuing, warning once per stall episode. The gate is re-evaluated every cycle with no latched state, so the monitor resumes automatically the instant HOST frees space or GPU pressure drops.
108:The monitor is not on the correctness-critical path: the pipeline executor drives downgrade on demand via `request_downgrade()` independently, so monitor back-off can never wedge a query. Monitor-issued requests are fire-and-forget.
110:### Downgrade Request Pattern
112:The downgrade executor uses a request-based model with tiered candidate fetching:
114:1. Caller invokes `request_downgrade(predicate)` which constructs a `downgrade_request` and pushes it onto the MPMC queue. Returns `std::future<size_t>`.
116:3. For each request, the processing loop fetches candidates lazily in tiered order:
117:   - **Tier 1 (data repositories):** Creates a `convertible_data_batch_provider` per repository and fetches idle GPU-resident batches one at a time
121:**Pipeline integration:** When `gpu_pipeline_executor` gets a partial memory reservation (shortfall), it issues a single `request_downgrade(predicate)` where the predicate attempts `make_reservation_or_null(bytes_needed)`. The downgrade stops as soon as the reservation succeeds -- single request, no over-freeing.
127:1. **Data repositories** are iterated in repository manager order. Within each repository, `convertible_data_batch_provider` iterates partitions back-to-front, then batches back-to-front, filtering for idle batches in the source memory space.
130:Candidates are converted individually via `convertible_data::convert()`, which handles state locking, memory reservation, tier conversion, and failure rollback atomically.

### 3A. Planning

#### P1 (confirmed). The six 1-CN failures are one FE plan shape: an unfiltered lineitem leaf feeding a hash-partitioned exchange, whose whole output must be parked on the GPU

**Measured.** In all six plans the failing fragment is a bare lineitem `FileScanNode` under a `HASH_PARTITIONED` `TDataStreamSink` with one destination (survey/plan-summary.txt lines 10, 16, 18, 34, 36, 42; dumps cn1/dump/fragment-0141 (q05, node 8), 0208 (q08), 0220 (q09), 0427 (q17, node 0), 0437 (q18, node 9), 0504 (q21, node 12), each `output_partition TPartitionType(2)` = HASH_PARTITIONED per `Partitions.thrift:41-49`). 265:### PR reviewability
266-
267-PRs sometimes stall for weeks after a reviewer is assigned, simply because the PR wasn't actually
268-ready to review the moment CODEOWNERS pinged someone. Before marking a PR ready for review, please
269-do the following:
270-
271-1. **State the motivation, not just the mechanics.** Link the originating issue (`Closes #NNN` /
272-   `Refs #NNN`) if one exists; if there isn't one, the description itself should explain *why* the
273-   change is needed, not just summarize the diff.
274-2. **Scope the PR to one reviewable sitting.** If a reviewer can't get through it start-to-finish
275-   without losing context, either split it (see [Stacked PRs](#stacked-prs)) or explicitly justify
276-   in the description why it can't be split.
277-3. **Make the description self-sufficient.** A reviewer should be able to start reviewing without
278-   needing to ask what changed or why — cover what changed, why, how it was verified, and anything
279-   non-obvious (e.g. "intentionally doesn't handle X, tracked in #NNN").
280-4. **Open as a draft until 1-3 are actually true**, then convert to "Ready for review" — that's
281-   the point CODEOWNERS review requests and author auto-assignment (`auto-assign.yml`) trigger, so
282-   converting early means a reviewer gets pinged before there's anything reviewable yet.
283-
284-### Commit and title convention
285-
286-Sirius squash-merges PRs, the PR titles become the commit message on merge. Commits and PR titles follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format for readability.
287-

289-```
290-<type>[optional scope]: <description>
291-
292-[optional body]
293-
294-[optional footer(s)]
295-```

1:## 3. Findings by dimension
7:#### P1 (confirmed). The six 1-CN failures are one FE plan shape: an unfiltered lineitem leaf feeding a hash-partitioned exchange, whose whole output must be parked on the GPU
40:#### P2 (confirmed). q02: the FE decorrelates the min-subquery into a full 800M-row partsupp chain and shuffles a 1-row region; its runtime filters are dropped by the CN
42:#### P5 (not adversarially verified). Semi/anti join sides, CTE inlining, lost operator fusion, dropped dynamic filters
55:#### Disputed planning finding
62:#### B1 (confirmed). Receiver-first rendezvous plus one fragment at a time turn every exchange into a full GPU materialisation
74:#### B2 (confirmed, mechanism sharpened). Parked batches are invisible to the downgrade sweep, so every OOM cycle frees 0 bytes although a 160 GiB HOST tier is configured
86:#### B3 (confirmed). The reschedule loop has no feasibility check: 179 stuck scan tasks x 100 retries x 50 ms, re-reading the split each time, while nothing can free memory
105:#### B4 (disputed: mechanism confirmed, causal claim refuted). Fragments of a failed query keep running and park output nobody consumes; the leak is 0-38 GB per failure but decided no pass/fail here
107:## 4. What to do first
130:## 5. Open questions and what was not measured

#### P1 (confirmed). The six 1-CN failures are one FE plan shape: an unfiltered lineitem leaf feeding a hash-partitioned exchange, whose whole output must be parked on the GPU

**Measured.** In all six plans the failing fragment is a bare lineitem `FileScanNode` under a `HASH_PARTITIONED` `TDataStreamSink` with one destination (survey/plan-summary.txt lines 10, 16, 18, 34, 36, 42; dumps cn1/dump/fragment-0141 (q05, node 8), 0208 (q08), 0220 (q09), 0427 (q17, node 0), 0437 (q18, node 9), 0504 (q21, node 12), each `output_partition TPartitionType(2)` = HASH_PARTITIONED per `Partitions.thrift:41-49`). The FE join labels differ (q05/q08/q09/q17 PARTITIONED, q18 `11:INNER JOIN (BUCKET_SHUFFLE(S))`, q21 `14:LEFT SEMI JOIN (BUCKET_SHUFFLE(S))`), the sink type does not. Lineitem is the build-side exchange in five plans and the probe-side exchange in q17. Every one of the six failing fragments was started as `role=sender inputs=0 outputs=1` (cn1/cluster.log lines 4200, 7854, 9840, 16770, 18095, 20282).

Because nothing streams across a fragment boundary (finding B1), the sender must park its entire projection. Size of that projection (standalone `GPU_SCAN in=` of the same scan, agent-notes/standalone-failed-quent.txt) versus what fit before the pool filled (cn1-quent.txt `STREAMING_SINK in=`, engine-cn0.log `[gpu_pool] QueryBegin/QueryEnd allocated=`):

| query | lineitem projection (GB) | pool before the sender started (GB) | parked by the sender at death (GB) | pool at death (GB) | stuck tasks x 100 retries |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| q05 | 171.00 | 0.00 | 104.30 | 104.30 | 25 |
| q08 | 195.75 | 4.70 (q05 leftovers) | 99.54 | 104.24 | 36 |
| q09 | 244.50 | 8.83 (q08 leftovers) | 96.42 | 105.24 | 56 |
| q17 | 122.25 | 38.16 (q09 + q16 leftovers) | 66.26 | 104.42 | 21 |
| q18 | 97.50 | 68.69 (own senders: customer 3.94 + agg 24.0 + orders 36.75, plus 4.0 q17 leftover) | 35.87 | 104.56 | 23 |
| q21 | 73.50 (the 28-task l2 leaf) | 77.76 (own filtered l1/l3 sender) | 25.37 | 103.14 | 18 |

Pool cap = 107,374,182,400 bytes (100 GiB); every one of the 17,917 OOM lines in cn1/engine-cn0.log reads `global usage 107374182400 bytes`. `begin + parked = end` holds within 0.01 GB in every row.

Correction to the original claim: "the sender cannot fit its own output" is true for q05/q08/q09/q17 (projection > 107 GB alone) but not for q18 (97.5 GB) or q21 (73.5 GB), which died because the query's other exchange inputs were parked at the same time. The accurate statement is: the sum of concurrently parked exchange inputs of one query (plus leftovers of earlier failed queries, finding B4) exceeds the pool, and nothing can be spilled (finding B2). Per-row widths in the engine are 12-41 B (decimals arrive as 8-byte values), so the analyst's "168-456 GB" range with decimal128 widths overstates three of the six.

**Measured, standalone contrast.** The same SQL on the same GPU and pool passes because DuckDB's stats-aware plan streams lineitem as the probe of a hash join built on the small filtered dimension chain: standalone-failed/runs/q05.explain.txt:50-61 has `READ_PARQUET lineitem ~6,110,827,680 rows` as the probe child with a ~61.6M-row build; q18.explain.txt:37-56 likewise; q17/q21 use DELIM joins. standalone-failed-quent q17 `HASH_JOIN(18) n=46 in=120.54 GB` shows lineitem probing in 46 batches, never materialised. Standalone still materialises lineitem-derived aggregate state (q18 PARTITION(5) 36.19 GB), just not the raw projection.

**Root cause.** `StatisticsCalculator.computeFileScanNode` (FE `sql/optimizer/statistics/StatisticsCalculator.java:664-676`): `// cause we don't know the real schema in file, just use the default Row Count now` `builder.setOutputRowCount(1)`, every column `ColumnStatistic.unknown()`. card-compare-cn1.txt shows FE estimate 1 for every exchange of the six queries against actuals of 150,000,000 / 227,571,151 (q05 s1/s4) and 730,806,711 (q21 s6). With every side at 1 row the CBO's fragment cut is arithmetic on column widths and node count (finding P3).

**Not measured.** Whether the six pass on 4 CNs. cn4/runs/runs.csv has no rows for them. A hash-partitioned exchange splits parked bytes across CNs (cn4 q03.r1: the 3.23B-row lineitem shuffle parked 19.60/19.67/19.71/19.86 GB per CN), so the per-CN lineitem share would be ~31-61 GB and the expected outcome is pass (inference). The 4-CN plans are also not identical: q21's `10:RIGHT ANTI JOIN` becomes `BUCKET_SHUFFLE(S)` with a local build (plan-summary-4cn.txt line 42).

**Proposed changes.**

1. FE: real FILES() cardinalities (finding C1, section 4 item 3). Caveat from the source skeptic (inference, medium confidence): with real statistics the small side of lineitem's join is orders-derived (q18 ~308M rows, q05 227M rows, tens of GB), `CostModel.java:428` multiplies a broadcast whose build exceeds `exec_mem_limit` (2 GiB, `SessionVariable.java:1305`) by `BROADCAST_JOIN_MEM_EXCEED_PENALTY` = 1000, and the shuffle network cost is 0 on a single node (`CostModel.java:437-440`). Real row counts alone may therefore still put lineitem across an exchange on 1 CN; this needs an `EXPLAIN COSTS` with statistics, which was not run.
2. CN, 1-CN only: fuse a leaf scan fragment into its single-destination receiver before translation, at the `TPlan` level (replace the receiver's `EXCHANGE_NODE` with the sender's node list; `ExchangeNode.java:183/360` guarantee the row layout matches). On 1 CN every exchange is local, so the fused plan is the standalone plan that passes all six. Substantial work; medium confidence. Caveat: for q21 the fused lineitem would sit on the build side of a `LEFT SEMI` that the translator cannot flip (no `RIGHT_SEMI`, finding P5), so q21 needs P5 as well.
3. Engine: fail fast (finding B3) so a wrong plan costs ~3 s instead of 54-232 s.

Confidence: high on the diagnosis; medium on which fix path is accepted.

#### P2 (confirmed). q02: the FE decorrelates the min-subquery into a full 800M-row partsupp chain and shuffles a 1-row region; its runtime filters are dropped by the CN

#### P5 (not adversarially verified). Semi/anti join sides, CTE inlining, lost operator fusion, dropped dynamic filters

These were analysed by one agent each and not refuted or confirmed by skeptics. Evidence is measured unless marked.

- **Semi/anti build side (PC-4, SAJ-2, SAJ-3).** q04: `5:LEFT SEMI JOIN (BROADCAST) build=4:EXCHANGE<-lineitem` with 3,793,363,900 rows (card-compare-cn1.txt line 20); 30.82 GB of `l_orderkey` parked (cn1-quent.txt q04 `STREAMING_SINK in=30.82GB`) and 22.76 GB shuffled on 4 CNs. The engine flips it internally: cn1/engine-cn0.log q04 F00 `HASH_JOIN (id=6) type: RIGHT_SEMI`, build = orders scan, probe = lineitem stream, so 1-CN time is at parity (1850 vs 1896 ms); the cost is memory and exchange volume, not time. q22: `11:LEFT ANTI JOIN (BROADCAST) build=10:EXCHANGE<-orders` 1.5B rows to every CN; per-CN `HASH_JOIN(15)` 0.516 s on 4 CNs vs 0.588 s on 1 CN (cn4-quent.txt q22.r1, cn1 q22.r0), which is why q22 scales 1.13x. Standalone uses `RIGHT_DELIM_JOIN RIGHT_ANTI` with the customer keys as build (standalone/runs/q22.explain.txt). The FE has the commutation rule (`rule/transformation/JoinCommutativityRule.java:34-44` LEFT_SEMI<->RIGHT_SEMI, LEFT_ANTI<->RIGHT_ANTI) but at cardinality 1 it never pays. The translator refuses `RIGHT_SEMI_JOIN` (`node_translator.rs:1743-1762`: the match has no RIGHT_SEMI arm, `_ => UnsupportedPlanNode "hash join type is unsupported"`) although the Substrait consumer (`substrait/src/from_substrait.cpp:558-560`) and the engine (`src/planner/sirius_plan_comparison_join.cpp:245,273`) support it. Proposed: add `TJoinOp::RIGHT_SEMI_JOIN => (JoinType::RightSemi, JoinOutput::Right)` plus a `JoinOutput::Right` arm; small, high confidence on feasibility.
- **Anti join emulation (SAJ-5).** `LEFT_ANTI_JOIN => (JoinType::Left, JoinOutput::LeftAnti)` at node_translator.rs:1749 is an outer join plus `IS NULL` filter because `from_substrait.cpp:540-570` lacks LEFT_ANTI/RIGHT_ANTI. Measured cost in q22: `HASH_JOIN(15) in=6.59GB` -> `FILTER(16) in=6.93GB` -> `PROJECTION(17) in=0.22GB` (cn1-ops.txt fragment 832d7f224fc8), i.e. ~97% of the join output is produced and discarded. Proposed: add the two cases to `SubstraitToDuckDB::TransformJoinOp` and map them natively (engine has `JoinType::ANTI`/`RIGHT_ANTI`, `sirius_plan_comparison_join.cpp:242-246`). Medium confidence.
- **CTE inlining (PC-5, MFS-1).** q15 scans lineitem twice in two fragments (cn1-quent.txt:990-1000: `GPU_SCAN n=56 in=122.25GB` in fragments 567 and 566, run times 2253 + 2163 ms strictly serial per cn1/cluster.log `fragment run started/finished`, agent-notes/multi-fragment-small.md section 3 (the Quent walls 4.434 / 2.149 s include the first fragment's parked wait); standalone one scan, 2627 vs 4685 ms); q11 runs the partsupp chain twice (16.4 GB + 13.1 GB). `CTEContext.needInline` (`sql/optimizer/CTEContext.java:157-190`) inlines unless cost*ratio says otherwise, and with 1-row stats inlining always wins (`cboCTERuseRatio = 1.15`, `SessionVariable.java:1511`). `SET cbo_cte_reuse_rate = 0` would force reuse (`isForceCTE`, CTEContext.java:206-217) but the CN refuses `MULTI_CAST_DATA_STREAM_SINK` by name (`compute_node_service.rs:1068`, `:1519`). This is also the plan-level cause of the q15 wrong answers (section 1).
- **q13 lost DENSE_COUNT_JOIN (SAJ-4).** FE plan: `5:HASH JOIN RIGHT OUTER -> 6:Project -> 7:AGGREGATE count(o_orderkey) group by c_custkey` (survey/explain/q13.costs.txt); the Substrait keeps the Project (cn1/dump/plan-0339.substrait: `aggregate -> project -> aggregate -> project -> join`); `detect_dense_count_join` (`src/planner/sirius_plan_aggregate.cpp`) requires the aggregate's direct child to be the join. Measured: CN `HASH_JOIN(6) 1.406 s + HASH_GROUP_BY(8) 0.261 s` in a 0.558 s fragment vs standalone `DENSE_COUNT_JOIN(4) 0.066 s` (cn1-ops.txt fragment 286810da3429; standalone-quent.txt); `grep -c "Fusing COUNT-join" cn1/engine-cn0.log` = 0. Proposed: look through a pure-column `LogicalProjection` in `detect_dense_count_join`, or elide the pure-subset PROJECT under an AGGREGATION_NODE in the translator. Medium confidence; it is ~0.4 s of q13's 0.38 s gap to standalone.

Standalone joins lineitem with the 8.69M delim keys below the aggregate (`DYNAMIC_FILTER(25)` on the scan) in 2.958 s. Proposed: implement remote runtime filters (as in P2) or, as an interim, honour the FE's STREAMING pre-aggregation mode as pass-through in `agg_phase.rs`. Medium confidence.
- **q07 dynamic filter no-op on the orders stream (FWJ-3).** cn1-ops.txt fragment 772c72f753ea: `DYNAMIC_FILTER(21)` on the 18.38 GB orders stream ran at +0.097 s, before its build published (Quent task timestamps), `PARTITION(22)` input 18.38 GB (no reduction), `HASH_JOIN(24) 0.753 s` vs standalone `HASH_JOIN(34) 0.072 s` with orders pre-filtered 18.37 -> 1.49 GB at the scan. On 4 CNs the planner logs `Not wiring dynamic filter(s): build side carries neither filter nor opaque-build evidence` (cn4/engine-.cn1.log 13:19:58.309). ~1.0 s of GPU operator time, ~0.25-0.3 s of wall in the join fragment. Proposed: treat a declared stream far below the base table as filter evidence (`src/planner/sirius_plan_comparison_join.cpp:646-664`) and add a dependency edge from the DF pipeline to the build's publish when the probe is a parked stream. Medium confidence.
- **The engine's in-fragment re-plan works, but only inside a fragment (PC-6).** Declared stream cardinalities equal actual parked rows for every stream (cn1-cnlog.txt `cards[]` vs card-compare), DuckDB reorders inner joins with them (q19: engine built on filtered part and probed the 128.6M-row lineitem stream, cn1-ops.txt 6493-6546; q07: build/probe of three joins flipped vs the FE), but `STATISTICS_PROPAGATION` is disabled (`src/sirius_ffi.cpp:233-240`), so a FILES() scan inside the same fragment keeps its raw estimate, and the fragment cut is fixed before any of this. Also see C2.
- **Two-phase aggregation is cheap (AGG-5).** q01/q06 merge and result fragments 3-24 ms, hops 1-7 ms, 20-40 ms total post-scan; parity 1.04/0.97. The translator's decimal lowering shifts ~0.5 s of summed GPU time into PROJECTION and is the 9.6e-4 deviation source. Low priority.

#### Disputed planning finding
======
#### B1 (confirmed). Receiver-first rendezvous plus one fragment at a time turn every exchange into a full GPU materialisation

**Source (verified).** `engine.rs:278-280`: `// One request at a time until the handle (and its sender) is dropped` `while let Ok(request) = requests.recv()`; `run_fragment_inner` (engine.rs:486-720) does declare -> `build()` -> `relay_from` each parked sender -> `run()` -> park (engine.rs:697-716). `src/sirius_ffi.cpp:739-745 relay_from` throws unless the source fragment has run. `local_exchange.rs:248-283 take_ready` returns a receiver only when every expected sender is complete. The remote path is also park-then-export (`EngineRequest::ExportNext`, engine.rs:91-95). Inside the engine, `Fragment::build()` opens a `StandaloneQueryScope` that takes the single-flight `query_lifecycle_mutex_` (`sirius_context.cpp:1555-1596`) until `run()` finishes, so two fragments cannot be in flight on one context even if the CN asked (source skeptic; this makes "run sender and receiver concurrently" engine work, not CN work).

**Measured, q05 timeline.** All 11 `exec_plan_fragment` RPCs arrived 13:03:43.358-43.462 (cn1/cluster.log 4142-4202). Fragments ran strictly sequentially: nation 6 ms, region 9 ms, then the lineitem sender 5774 started 13:03:43.434 with `allocated=2304 bytes` (engine-cn0.log:49203, an empty pool) and parked 39 batches x 2.668 GB = 104.06 GB by +1.315 s (Quent data_batch Stationary events: 26.7 GB at +0.32 s, 66.7 GB at +0.88 s); first OOM at +1.361 s (engine-cn0.log:49221 `requested 748875880 bytes ... global usage 107374182400 bytes (102400.00 MB), peak allocated 3376381184, reservation 3318948864`). The supplier/customer/orders fragments started only after the failure at 13:05:24.632+ (cluster.log 6072-6305); the receiver of streams 7 and 9 never started (Quent shows 7 of 11 fragments). Receiver 5775 later ran in 73 ms and its output sat parked for 184.5 s until q08's failure wipe (cn1-quent.txt wall=184.502 s, Comp=0.128 s).

**Measured, passing queries show the same shape under the cap.** cn1 q07.r0: all 7 senders finished before the join fragment started (cluster.log 6807-7005); 59.47 GB of lineitem plus 18.38 GB of orders were parked (79.1 GB, 74% of the pool) with dwell up to 2.76 s. cn4 q07.r1: every `fragment run finished` precedes its first `transmitted batches via nixl`. Per-fragment run sums vs span (MFS-4): cn1 q02.r1 13 fragments sum 977 ms, span 1067 ms, gaps 90 ms (8%); cn4 q02.r1 cn0 sum 748 ms, span 1081 ms, gaps 333 ms (31%), the largest before receivers waiting for the other CNs' senders. The 4-slot executor idles during the many 1-task fragments (cn1 q02.r1: 133 tasks, Comp 2.9 s in a 1.06 s span = 2.7 of 4 slots busy).

**Streaming works within a fragment.** q21 fragment 2acb (ran after the failure) streamed a 123 GB lineitem scan through FILTER -> HASH_JOIN in 3.15 s with only 46.47 GB partitioned out (cn1-quent.txt q21.r0). Only the exchange forces full materialisation.

**Proposed.** Two routes: (1) on 1 CN, fuse local-only fragments before translation (P1, item 2); every exchange is local, the fused plan is the standalone plan, no engine change. (2) Streaming receivers: build once build-side streams are complete, consume probe-side streams while the sender still runs, run sender and receiver concurrently. (2) requires per-fragment lifecycle/task creators in the engine (the single-flight `query_lifecycle_mutex_` and the shared `task_creator_` reset in `begin_execution_window`, `sirius_context.cpp:392-395`) and a build/probe decision before the streamed side's cardinality is known. Confidence high on the mechanism; medium (1) and low-medium (2) on design effort.

#### B2 (confirmed, mechanism sharpened). Parked batches are invisible to the downgrade sweep, so every OOM cycle frees 0 bytes although a 160 GiB HOST tier is configured

**Measured.** cn1/engine-cn0.log: 17,917 lines `[downgrade] [GPU:0] downgrade request not satisfied and disk memory space is not configured; data cannot be spilled to disk` and 17,917 `after downgrade (0 bytes freed), reservation still partial (...) -- proceeding with partial reservation`; per query 2503/3603/5603/2103/2302/1803. Zero lines with non-zero bytes freed. `[host_pool] HOST:0 ... allocated=72351744` is constant through the q05 storm (the host tier exists: `HOST_MEM=160GiB` -> `sirius.memory.host.capacity_bytes`, `engine_settings.rs:111-116`; `1 host memory space(s) created`). The bench kit already documents "host spill is NOT implemented" (`benchmarks/tpch/run-abc.sh:1038`).

**Source (verified).** `src/exec/streaming_fragment.cpp:103-112`: `// Repositories escape data_repository_manager_ cleanup so sender output outlives this fragment.` `_output_repos[id] = std::make_shared<cucascade::shared_data_repository>()` (and `_input_repos` likewise). The only registration path into a per-query manager is `repository_wiring_materializer.cpp:68-71 add_new_repository` (inter-pipeline ports). `src/downgrade/downgrade_executor.cpp:223-232` TIER 1 iterates `_data_repo_registry.get_all()` managers only; `:294-300` TIER 2 the pipeline task queue (queued GPU_SCAN tasks hold no input batches). The warning at `:357-363` fires whenever no DISK tier exists and the request is unsatisfied, regardless of whether any candidate existed. `src/sirius_ffi.cpp:1062-1066 output_row_count` throws on a non-GPU-resident parked batch (the CN swallows it with `.ok()` and plans blind, engine.rs:564, 582-585); `:822-825 export_packed` throws too, which would fail the 4-CN path on a spilled batch.

**Correction.** The original clause "the sender's engine query has already ended" is not the operative reason. In q05/q08/q09 the bytes that filled the pool (104.30/99.54/96.42 GB) are the *running* leaf fragment's own STREAMING_SINK output; its query and manager existed, but a `GPU_SCAN -> STREAMING_SINK` fragment registers no repository at all. Finished-sender outputs account for 0 / 4.7 / 8.8 GB in those three, 38.2 / 68.7 / 77.8 GB in q17/q18/q21. The escape from the manager is the whole mechanism, and the receiver's `_input_repos` are equally invisible.

**Impact arithmetic (inference).** Spilled data has to fit GPU + HOST = 107.4 + 171.8 = 279 GB. Totals a working spill would have to hold: q17 ~160 GB, q18 ~166, q05 ~171, q21 ~195, q08 ~200, q09 ~253. Five of six would plausibly pass slowly; q09 is marginal after the 16 GiB staging arena and the ~34 GB host-pool peak. The original "host spill rescues only q17/q18" compared against the host tier alone and should be dropped.

**Proposed.** Register the streaming sink's output repositories and the receiver's input repositories with a process-level registry the downgrade executor sweeps as a third tier, including the running fragment's own sink (otherwise q05/q08/q09 still die). Make `Fragment::output_row_count` read a row count from host metadata and `export_packed` accept HOST-tier batches (the local relay already upgrades HOST -> GPU in `lock_or_prepare_batch`). Correct the warning to distinguish "no convertible candidates" from "no disk tier". Note the newest-first fairness policy at `downgrade_executor.cpp:204-216`; the candidate that matters here is the newest fragment's own output. Confidence high on the mechanism, medium that spill is worth doing before P1/B1.

#### B3 (confirmed). The reschedule loop has no feasibility check: 179 stuck scan tasks x 100 retries x 50 ms, re-reading the split each time, while nothing can free memory
